intro: Out in Kaditz a lime that half burned down in 1818 still stands, held up from inside by roots that turned into stems. It is probably Dresden's oldest tree. Its rival is a giant oak in the Dresdner Heide, listed as a boundary marker in 1679 and now patched with concrete. In town stand a splinter-scarred oak in the Grosser Garten, an overcup oak with a 1949 tram shelter built around it, and an elm that came through Dutch elm disease. At Laubegast, a riverside lime still carries the scar of the 1940 Elbe ice.
meta_description: Thirteen notable Dresden trees: a lime in Kaditz that half burned in 1818, a Heide oak recorded in 1679, and a riverside lime scarred by the 1940 ice.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Dresden is the Kaditzer Linde, a large-leaved lime in the churchyard of the Emmauskirche in Kaditz, and the city itself declines to say how old. Its sign calls the tree many centuries old and then adds a thousand years with a question mark, because a fire in 1818 destroyed the side of the trunk facing the parsonage and no ring count has been possible since. What stands there now is a half shell over nine metres round, held up on the inside by former roots that turned into supporting stems. Estimates in the literature run from 500 to 1000 years. Its nearest rival on this page is the Rieseneiche in the Sauerbusch, a pedunculate oak in the Dresdner Heide that a forest record of 1679 already listed as a boundary marker, estimated at up to 700 years. Next comes the lime on the Laubegast riverbank, planted or sown around 1680. If you know of a dated study that narrows the lime's age, tell us.
question_meta: The Kaditzer Linde, a lime in the Kaditz churchyard, is Dresden's oldest: estimates run from 500 to 1000 years and the city's own sign asks the question.
question_context: Dresden keeps an official register of natural monuments, Naturdenkmale, reproduced as a public Wikipedia table alongside dedicated articles for several individual trees and, for five of the trees here, cross-checked against Stadtwiki Dresden, an independent community wiki that lists the same trees by their own register numbers. Nine of the thirteen trees on this page carry that formal designation. The Splittereiche does not, protected instead as part of the listed historic Grosser Garten around it, and the Luthereiche is a Saxon Kulturdenkmal rather than a Naturdenkmal; the Saengereiche and the Bismarckeiche have no official designation. The Albertplatz plane and the Fetscherplatz oak were designated by the same council resolution of 3 January 1985; the Trinitatisplatz oak waited until February 2024. The Kaditzer Linde is the exception: probably the oldest, 6 km northwest of the old town, and carrying a range rather than an estimate, because the trunk has been too damaged for too long to be counted. Several other ages come from a planting date recorded at designation, which beats a growth-rate guess and is still not a ring count; the Rieseneiche's is an estimate, and the Konigsbrucker Strasse elm has no recorded age at all.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Dresden?
faq.a: The Kaditzer Linde, a large-leaved lime in the churchyard of the Emmauskirche in Kaditz. Estimates run from 500 to 1000 years and the city's own sign puts a question mark after the higher figure, because a fire in 1818 destroyed half the trunk and left nothing to count.

faq.q: Can I see all thirteen trees in one walk?
faq.a: No. The Zerr-Eiche and the Fetscherplatz oak both stand in Johannstadt, a short tram ride apart, and Albertplatz, the Konigsbrucker Strasse elm and the oak at the Barnsdorfer Strasse fork sit north of the river in the Neustadt. The Grosser Garten, the Laubegast lime on the Elbe and Kaditz, 6 km northwest of the old town, are each a trip of their own, and the Rieseneiche is a forest walk in the far north-east of the Dresdner Heide.
Yes. All thirteen stand on open public squares and streets, in a public park, in a churchyard, beside a riverside cycle path or in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide, with no ticket needed.

faq.q: Why are several of these trees protected under the same 1985 date?
faq.a: Dresden's city council designated the Albertplatz plane and the Fetscherplatz oak as natural monuments in a single resolution on 3 January 1985. The Trinitatisplatz oak had to wait far longer, gaining the same protection only in February 2024.

trees.name: The Zerr-Eiche of Trinitatisplatz

location.address: Trinitatisplatz, opposite the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche, Johannstadt, Dresden

trees.access: Free, standing on a public square (Trinitatisplatz) opposite the church
trees.transport: Tram stop Trinitatisplatz, right on the square (news coverage of a nearby tram diversion names conflicting line numbers across sources, so no specific line is stated here)
trees.story:
Dresden got round to protecting this oak in February 2024, some 130 years after the city planted it. It was raised at the municipal nursery on the Tatzberg and set out on Trinitatisplatz in 1895, facing the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche. Fifty years later the air raids of February 1945 came over Johannstadt, and the oak came through them without serious damage. It then came through the winters that followed, when firewood was scarce enough in Dresden that standing trees disappeared into stoves, and this one was left alone.

It is a Turkey oak, a southern European species with deeply cut leaves and acorns sitting in shaggy, mossy cups rather than the smooth ones a German oak wears. The case for designating it called it the strongest of its kind in Dresden and the third strongest in Saxony, on grounds of age, rarity, form and genetic value.

The trunk measures about 3.84 metres round, worked from a recorded stem diameter of 122 centimetres, although the city's own register line says more than four metres. Nobody has reconciled the two figures and neither is worth much fuss.

Twenty metres tall, standing in the open on a public square with a tram stop at its foot, it is about as easy to reach as a protected tree gets.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak facing the main portal of the Trinitatiskirche across Trinitatisplatz, with a tram stop at its foot.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Albertplatz

location.address: Albertplatz, on the traffic island toward Bautzner Strasse, Innere Neustadt, Dresden

trees.access: Free, standing on a traffic island in the middle of a public square, accessible at any time
trees.transport: Albertplatz tram and bus interchange, right on the square
trees.story:
This plane tree lives on a traffic island. Albertplatz is one of the busiest interchanges in Dresden, a circle of tram and bus routes in the Neustadt, and the tree stands out in the middle of it toward Bautzner Strasse, twenty-five metres tall with a crown roughly as wide as it is high.

It was planted around 1885, when that ground was open and quiet. Everything else arrived later: the trams, the traffic, the night of 13 February 1945 and the long rebuilding after it, forty years of the GDR, and the Neustadt's more recent turn into the loudest quarter in the city. The tree has stayed put through all of it on its own island, which is the closest thing to a fixed point Albertplatz has. Dresden made it a natural monument on 3 January 1985, by the same council resolution that protected the oak on Fetscherplatz.

A London plane is a hybrid of the American and the Oriental plane, and it was planted across European cities for exactly the qualities on show here. It takes heat, compacted soil and dirty air better than almost anything else with a trunk, and it sheds its bark in pale plates through the summer instead of letting the grime build up.

Its trunk measures 3.30 metres round. Both the register and the city's own record agree on the figure, which is rarer than it sounds.

photo.note: good whole-tree frame of a plane on Albertplatz, but 35 m, no register id, and a large square that may hold more than one plane

trees.how_to_recognise: The plane tree standing alone on the traffic island toward Bautzner Strasse, in the middle of the Albertplatz interchange.

trees.name: The Oak of Fetscherplatz
trees.access: Free, standing on a public square, visible and reachable at all times
trees.transport: Tram stop Fetscherplatz, directly beside the tree
trees.story:
In 1949 an architect built a tram shelter around this tree rather than move either of them. Herbert Schneider put his waiting kiosk on Fetscherplatz so close to the trunk that the roof had to curve to make room for the oak, four years after the air raids, in a city with more urgent things to be careful about. The two have shared the corner ever since.

The tree is an overcup oak, a North American species and an unlikely thing to find holding down a square in Johannstadt. It went in around 1900, when the place was still called Fuerstenplatz, and it has since put out a crown about thirty-two metres across, wider than the tree is tall. That crown is effectively the roof of the square. Twenty-five metres up, 3.35 metres round at the trunk, and the only real shade anyone waiting for a tram is going to get.

Dresden protected it as a natural monument on 3 January 1985, in the same council resolution that covered the plane tree on Albertplatz.

If you are there in autumn, look at the acorns on the ground. The cup on this species swallows almost the entire nut, which is where the name comes from and the quickest way to tell it apart from every other oak in the city.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak whose crown roofs Fetscherplatz, with a curved 1949 tram shelter built up against its trunk.

trees.name: The Splittereiche

location.address: Grosser Garten, on the open lawn roughly 40 metres south of the Mosaikbrunnen (Mosaic Fountain), Dresden

trees.access: Free, standing in the open on a public lawn inside the Grosser Garten park, open during park hours
trees.transport: Enter the Grosser Garten and walk to the Mosaikbrunnen; nearest tram stops are around Strassburger Platz or Lenneplatz, roughly a 10-15 minute walk into the park (approximate, not independently timed)
trees.story:
This oak is named after its wounds. On the nights of 13 and 14 February 1945 the bombing of Dresden reached the Grosser Garten, and splinters tore open one side of the trunk along roughly eight metres of its height. The tree survived. The damage is still there and still obvious, which is how it came to be called the Splittereiche, the splinter oak.

It was already old when that happened. An assessment made in the 2010s put it at between 250 and 300 years, a range nobody has narrowed since and which is itself a decade out of date by now. It stands twenty-seven metres tall with a trunk over six metres round, out on open lawn a short walk south of the Mosaikbrunnen, so you see the whole shape of it from a distance before you get to the scar.

On 8 May 2017, the seventy-second anniversary of the end of the war in Europe, a memorial plaque went up beside it carrying a line from Mark Twain: time may heal all wounds, but it is a lousy cosmetician. The year after, the city fitted metal sheeting over the damaged flank, because visitors picking at the old injury were making it worse.

We have not found it listed individually in Dresden's register of natural monuments. It stands inside a protected historic park instead, and it is the tree people in that park come to find.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak on the open lawn south of the Mosaikbrunnen, with a visible bomb-splinter scar running up one side and a 2017 memorial plaque beside it.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Kaditzer Linde
trees.age_estimate: somewhere between 500 and 1000 years; the city's own sign asks the question rather than answering it
trees.story:
Half of this tree burned in 1818 and what holds the other half up is its own roots.

A fire that year took eighteen farms, thirty barns and the parsonage of Kaditz, and the lime beside the church went with them. The side facing the parsonage died outright. What survived is a half shell of trunk, and the city's sign on it explains the trick that kept the thing alive: the stems standing inside the hollow are former roots that turned into supports.

Dresden calls it the oldest tree in the city and will not put a number on it. The sign says many centuries old, then adds a thousand years with a question mark after it. Nothing can be counted, because the trunk has been damaged too often for rings to survive. A parish account of 1909 put the circumference at twelve and a half metres. A measurement at chest height in 2007 gave 9.6. Both figures are in the record and nobody has reconciled them.

Since 1829 its heaviest limbs have been held up, first on timber, now on steel anchors and cables. The smaller of its two stems stopped leafing out in 2021 and died. The larger one did not.

A bench runs in a ring around the base.
trees.access: Free. In the churchyard of the Emmauskirche, open in daylight. A wooden bench rings the trunk.
trees.transport: Tram 9 to its terminus at Kaditz, Riegelplatz, then about ten minutes on foot into Altkaditz. About 6 km northwest of the old town.

photo.attribution: DynaMoToR, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: Not a trunk but a standing half shell, wide open on one side, with a curved wooden bench built around its foot and steel cables running up into the crown. A war memorial with a stone eagle stands a few metres away.

trees.name: The Rieseneiche of the Sauerbusch

location.address: Sauerbusch, Dresdner Heide (forest district Hofewiese), near Langebruck

trees.access: Free. Public forest (Sachsenforst, Dresdner Heide); a signposted educational trail 'Rieseneichen' (run by the Heimatverein Weixdorf) leads to it. Forest paths, no ticket.
trees.transport: Not verified. Remote forest stand in the far north-east of the Heide near Langebruck, well over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot or by bike from Langebruck or Weixdorf. Check current timetables before quoting a stop.
trees.story:
In 1679 a forest protocol listed two oaks in the Sauerbusch as boundary markers. One of them is still alive. Its main stem broke off at about fifteen metres long ago, so what stands now is a trunk about 6.60 metres round carrying a crown made of single limbs. The local account puts it at up to 700 years, which is an estimate rather than a count; somewhere between four and seven centuries is the honest reading.

The two oaks were probably mast trees, kept for their acorns, and both were placed under protection in 1938, although some sources give 1958. In 1993 a fire started by children killed the second one. This one carried on.

It has not carried on easily. The forest district describes it as being in the last stage of its life, although it is still vital. Heavy growth covers the stem, one side is almost stripped of bark, and parts of it are held together with concrete. Even its height is disputed: the Wikipedia article says about 22 metres, the city's natural monument list says 14.

A signposted trail, the Rieseneichen path kept by the heritage society in Weixdorf, leads through the far north-east of the Dresdner Heide to the trunk. It is a forest walk from Langebruck or Weixdorf rather than a city stroll, and this oak is the reason to make it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the snapped-off main stem on a trunk about 6.60 metres round, one side almost bare of bark and patched with concrete. It stands on the signposted Rieseneichen trail in the Sauerbusch.
trees.verify_notes: Register-only (city Naturdenkmal ND 72; de.wikipedia plus Wikidata coordinate). Tree-level Wikidata coordinate; Commons has CC0 photos of the trunk base and hole taken 2021-05-31 by Pedalito (CC0), so a photo exists; lifecheck RECENT 2025-06-12 near the pin. Conflict on height: de.wikipedia article says about 22 m, the ND list says 14 m; main stem broke off at about 15 m, the crown is single limbs. Girth about 6.60 m at 1.30 m (measured 2016, cited to monumentaltrees on the list page; cross-checked on article). Age 'up to 700 years' is an estimate in the article, not a measured date; keep vague. History: 1679 forest protocol lists two oaks in the Sauerbusch as boundary markers, likely mast trees; both protected 1938 (other sources say 1958); the second oak fell in a fire started by children in 1993. The forest district describes the tree as 'in its last stage of life' although vital; stem has heavy overgrowth, one side nearly debarked, parts stabilised with concrete. Alive as of 2021 photos; recheck. Twin folded: none (the second oak is gone). Lead: a 'Dresdner Heide' walk with the Rotbuche dre_007 (about 5.5 km apart, separate stops).

trees.name: The Oak of Barnsdorfer Strasse

location.address: Junction of Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse, Leipziger Vorstadt

trees.access: Free. A freestanding tree at a street junction on public ground.
trees.transport: Not verified in detail; inner-city district north-west of the Neustadt, on the B170 side near Hansastrasse. Check the nearest tram stop before quoting.
trees.story:
This oak probably started out in a beer garden. It was planted around 1880 on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork, and the pub on that tip, Zur Gruenen Aue, stood until 1960. The written record says the tree was probably part of the pub's garden, and nobody has managed to get further than probably. The pub is gone. The oak, about 140 years old, has outlasted it by more than sixty years.

It has grown to about 25 metres with a crown some 30 metres wide, and its trunk measures 4.45 metres round. Dresden made it a natural monument on 3 January 1985, the same day the city protected the Kaditzer Linde, an oak on Doebelner Strasse and a pine in the Heide.

About 150 metres to the north-east, in the St.-Pauli-Friedhof, stand two more oaks of the same generation, the Marschall oak and the Meschwitz oak, planted around 1870 or 1880 and treated by the city as memorial trees. We have not checked how freely the cemetery can be walked, so this page sends you only to the junction.

The newest photographs of this oak date from 2015, and we have no recent confirmation that it is still in good health. If you pass the fork and it is standing, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the freestanding oak, 4.45 metres round, on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork. It stands about 100 metres south-east of where Hechtstrasse leaves Hansastrasse.
trees.verify_notes: Register only (city Naturdenkmal ND 29, protected 3 Jan 1985, resolution 266/85). Tree-level Wikidata coordinate; de.wikipedia places it at the southern fork of Weinbohlaer and Barnsdorfer Strasse, about 100 m south-east of the Hechtstrasse turn-off from Hansastrasse, which fits the pin. Photos: 8 files CC BY-SA 3.0 Dr. Bernd Gross, 2015-05-20. lifecheck on the pin returned NONE and the newest photo is 2015, so alive confirmation is thin: flagged. Height about 25 m, crown about 30 m, girth 4.45 m (register). Planted about 1880, probably in the beer garden of the pub 'Zur Gruenen Aue' on the road tip, which stood until 1960 (article says 'vermutlich', so keep hedged; do not bridge it into fact). About 150 m north-east, in the St.-Pauli-Friedhof, stand the Marschall oak and Meschwitz oak, planted c.1870/80 and treated as Dresden memorial trees (Wikidata Q109422836, Q124842660): possible cluster, not verified as accessible here. Protected the same day as the Doebelner Strasse oak, the Kaditzer Linde (dre_005) and the Heide pine.

trees.name: The Linden on the Laubegast Riverbank

location.address: Laubegaster Ufer, by house no. 17, Altlaubegast

trees.access: Free. Stands on the outside of the ice-protection wall of Laubegaster Ufer 17, beside the road; just north of the driveway the road is closed to cars and is a foot and cycle path forming part of the left-bank Elbe cycle route.
trees.transport: Not verified; Laubegast is an eastern Elbe-bank district. Check the nearest tram stop and walking time before quoting.
trees.story:
In March 1940 the biggest Elbe flood of the twentieth century drove ice floes 40 centimetres thick against this lime for ten to fifteen hours. The floes hit both the tree and the masonry surround its owner had built in 1913. The ice tore a wound about half a metre tall around half the trunk, and the ridge it left still shows at roughly 1.5 metres up.

The lime was already old by then. The local account has it planted or sown in the second half of the seventeenth century, most likely in the 1670s or around 1680, and in 1997 the owner wrote of a 320-year-old linden. That puts it somewhere near 340 today. The house behind it at number 17 is a youngster by comparison, built in 1879 for a Saxon court marshal and now a listed monument in its own right.

It is a small-leaved lime, about 20 metres tall with a trunk 3.90 metres round, standing outside the ice-protection wall beside the road. The paving over its roots was replaced with cobbles to protect them, and the city made it a natural monument in June 1999.

Just north of the driveway the road closes to cars and becomes part of the Elbe cycle route, and two more protected trees stand about 500 metres away in each direction along it: black poplars at number 1 and a black pine at number 39.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers and the riverbank smells of lime blossom

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the old ice wound, a ridge at about 1.5 metres on a trunk 3.90 metres round. It stands by the road outside the wall of Laubegaster Ufer 17.
trees.verify_notes: Register (city Naturdenkmal ND 89, protected 10 June 1999) plus the owner's 1997 letter quoted on de.wikipedia. Coordinates: de.wikipedia list 51/1/30.95N 13/50/23.9E (=51.02582, 13.83997), Wikidata Q124719169 51.0253,13.839993; they agree within about 70 m, so I used the list value which is described as 'by Nr. 17'; stated confirmed because the tree is on the Elbe path next to a named house, but a writer could re-read the Wikidata offset. Alive: Commons photo 2025-12-27 by Z thomas (CC BY 4.0) and 2024-05-09 lifecheck RECENT. Girth 3.90 m, height about 20 m, crown about 16 m. Age: article says planted or sown in the second half of the 17th century, narrowing to the 1670s or 1680, and the owner wrote of a '320 year old' linden in 1997. The owner built a protective masonry surround in 1913. In March 1940 the largest Elbe flood of the 20th century drove 40 cm ice floes against the wall and tree for 10 to 15 hours, leaving a wound about 50 cm tall around half the trunk; a ridge at roughly 1.5 m height still shows it. Pavement around the roots was replaced with cobbles to protect it. The house behind was built 1879 for a Saxon court marshal (protected Kulturdenkmal). Two other Laubegast ND trees stand about 500 m each way (black poplars at no. 1, black pine at no. 39), same cycle path. Photos CC BY-SA 3.0 Dr. Bernd Gross 2014/2015.

trees.name: The Fluttering Elm of Konigsbrucker Strasse

location.address: Konigsbrucker Strasse 49, on the pavement side between houses 49 and 51, Aussere Neustadt

trees.access: Free. The elm stands on the pavement side of the property in front of the houses at Konigsbrucker Strasse 49 to 51 and is visible and reachable from the public pavement on a main street; the pin marks the tree on the street frontage.
trees.transport: Not verified in detail; Aussere Neustadt on the Konigsbrucker Strasse tram corridor, close to the centre. Check the nearest stop before quoting.
trees.story:
Dresden protected this elm in 2015 for surviving something most of its kind have not. Dutch elm disease, spread by fungi that arrived from Asia, has killed elms across Europe, and when the city went looking in the early 2010s for its most valuable trees, 39 of them at 29 sites, it picked this European white elm as an exceptional specimen that was still healthy.

It is not a park tree. It stands on Konigsbrucker Strasse in the Aussere Neustadt, on the pavement side in front of numbers 49 and 51, and it sets the look of the street: about 30 metres tall, with a crown some 20 metres across and a trunk 3.57 metres round. Trams run past it along the Konigsbrucker Strasse corridor.

It was not the city's first protected elm. A white elm in Altubigau and the elms on Sachsenplatz had been natural monuments since 1999, so this one joined a short list rather than starting it.

Two things we do not know. Nobody has documented when it was planted, so this page gives no age; if you know, tell us. And the newest photographs on record are from 2019, so if you walk past and it is still standing over the pavement, that is worth a message too.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall elm, about 30 metres, on the pavement side of Konigsbrucker Strasse in front of numbers 49 and 51. Its trunk measures 3.57 metres round.
trees.verify_notes: Register (city Naturdenkmal ND 131, ordinance January 2015). Wikidata coordinate 51.07062119,13.74958807 matches the ND list value 51/4/14.05N 13/44/59.05E (=51.07057, 13.74974), two independent entries within about 15 m. Photos: 5 files CC BY-SA 3.0 Z thomas 2018-05-28 and 7 files 2019-05-06/07, plus Dr. Bernd Gross 2015. lifecheck says OLD (2011 file) but the Commons upload dates show 2018/2019; newest photo 2019, so alive-now is thin: flagged. Measurements per de.wikipedia: height about 30 m, crown about 20 m, girth 3.57 m. Why it was chosen: in the early 2010s the city put forward 39 especially valuable trees at 29 sites for protection; this elm was picked because European elm species are threatened by Dutch elm disease from Asian fungi and this exceptional specimen is healthy and defines the streetscape. Flatter-Ulme Altubigau and the Sachsenplatz elms had been protected since 1999. No age is documented; leave empty and let the page ask. Possible access caveat: the tree is on the property frontage 'gehwegseitig vorgelagert' (pavement-side), which I read as public pavement; I could not check the plot boundary on the ground.

trees.name: The Rotbuche of the Dresdner Heide

location.address: Dresdner Heide, forest section 109 (Revier Langebruck), about 150 m north-west of the crossing of Radeberger Strasse and Schneise 8

trees.access: Free. Stands in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide (Sachsenforst), a short way off the Schneise 8 forest ride; no entry charge.
trees.transport: Not verified. Inside the Heide, over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot from the Radeberger Strasse side. Check timetables before quoting a stop.
trees.verify_notes: Register only (city Naturdenkmal ND 108, designated Dec 2000). Wikidata coordinate 51.09819,13.849767 agrees with the de.wikipedia description (150 m NW of the Radeberger Strasse / Schneise 8 crossing) only in prose, which I did not measure, so precision is stated approximate. Photos on Commons: CC BY-SA 3.0 by Dr. Bernd Gross (2015-05-26, 22 files) and CC BY-SA 4.0 Staubi59 (2017). lifecheck on the pin returned NONE. Measurements at designation in 2000: height about 35 m, girth 5.70 m, crown diameter about 28 m. After an unseen fork defect plus a hurricane in October 2002 more than a third of the crown broke off, so today's tree is lower and lopsided; the 35 m figure is the pre-2002 height. The photos show the tree after the damage, which a writer should check. Age 250 years was an estimate in 2000. At designation only the beech behind the Weisses Schloss in Cossebaude (ND 66) was a bigger beech in Dresden. Protected zone 18 m around the trunk.
trees.story:
In October 2002 a hurricane found a fork in this beech that nobody knew was failing, and more than a third of the crown came down. Two years earlier Dresden had made it a natural monument, measured at about 35 metres tall, 5.70 metres round and with a crown some 28 metres across. At that point only one beech in the city was bigger, the one behind the Weisses Schloss in Cossebaude.

What stands in forest section 109 of the Dresdner Heide today is the tree that came out of that storm: lower than the 35 metres in the record and lopsided where the crown went. Every photograph on file was taken after the damage, so they show the beech as a visitor will meet it rather than as it looked on the day it was designated.

The age given in 2000 was about 250 years, and that was an estimate then. Add the years since and it lands somewhere around 275, give or take a few decades. The ordinance protects a ring of 18 metres around the trunk along with the tree itself.

It stands a short way into the forest, about 150 metres north-west of the point where Radeberger Strasse crosses the forest ride called Schneise 8. Our pin is approximate, so expect to look around for the broken crown once you reach the crossing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lopsided crown, more than a third of it lost to a storm in 2002, above a trunk about 5.70 metres round. It stands about 150 metres north-west of where Radeberger Strasse crosses Schneise 8.

photo.attribution: Dr. Bernd Gross, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Sängereiche on the Elbe Meadows

location.address: Elbwiesen (Waldschlösschenwiese), beside the Waldschlösschenbrücke and the Körnerweg / Elbe cycle path, Radeberger Vorstadt

trees.access: Free. Stands on the open public Elbe meadows beside the asphalted Körnerweg / Elbe cycle path; no entry, open at all times.
trees.transport: Not timetable-verified. Neustadt bank of the Elbe at the Waldschlösschenbrücke; the Bautzner Strasse stops on the plateau above are roughly 10 to 15 minutes on foot down to the meadows (check stops before quoting).

photo_candidate.note: Description names the tree and its position beside the Waldschlösschenbrücke; also on the same tree: File:Dresden, Waldschlößchenbrücke, Elberadweg, 17.6.2.40-080367.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0, Albrecht Voss, 3 Aug 2022, geotag 51.06625,13.77740, 14 m from the pin). Not viewed by me; the viewing pass must look at the pixels.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the oak standing on its own on the widest part of the meadow, its trunk over four metres round. It stands about 25 metres east of the Waldschlösschenbrücke railing, just north of the cycle path.
trees.verify_notes: Pin: OSM node 5620261952 (natural=tree, name Sängereiche, wikidata-linked) at 51.0661121,13.7773475, Wikidata P625 51.066125,13.777365 (about 2 m apart; the Wikidata point derives from the OSM node, so they are not fully independent). A geotagged Commons photo of this tree (Albrecht Voss 2022) lies 14 m away, and the dewiki article places it about 25 m from the bridge railing on the meadow at its widest point. Several unnamed OSM trees stand 20 to 50 m away, which is why the named node and photo description carry the pin. Facts (de.wikipedia, citing Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv): memorial oak for the first German Sängerbundesfest, July 1865 (Dresden); planted 13 Nov 1865 where the festival hall had stood, by Heinrich Hartwig with two gardeners. 1994: height 26 m, crown 20 m, girth 3.80 m; 2018 girth 4.26 m (girth_cm 426 is the 2018 figure; height_m 26 is the 1994 figure). The 1925 festival booklet says the November 1865 tree was the original gift (Leipzig-area choirs carried a young oak in a tub in the procession) and that a replanting was later needed after vandalism; Rainer Pfannkuchen (ex head of Dresden's nature-protection authority, Elbhang-Kurier April 2021) thinks the original died of drought and the 1865 planting was already a replacement. So the age basis is the documented November 1865 planting, but whether today's trunk is that planting or a later replacement is disputed in the sources: say so, keep the age as an estimate. Not a Naturdenkmal (no ND number found). Alive: photographed 2022 (Commons geotag), girth measured 2018, discussed 2021. lifecheck.py returned OLD (2010) only because it sees bridge-construction photos; the 2022 Commons file is the better evidence. The Waldschlösschenbrücke opened 2013 and the tree stands about 25 m from it. No official register: dewiki plus OSM plus Commons, flagged.
trees.story:
This oak was planted for a song festival, and the sources still argue over whether it is the oak they planted. In July 1865 Dresden hosted the first German Sängerbundesfest, and a festival hall went up on this stretch of the Elbe meadows. On 13 November that year, according to the Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv, Heinrich Hartwig and two gardeners planted a memorial oak where the hall had stood.

That is where the agreement ends. A festival booklet from 1925 says the November tree was the singers' own gift, a young oak that choirs from around Leipzig had carried through the procession in a tub, and that it later had to be replaced after vandals got to it. Rainer Pfannkuchen, once head of Dresden's nature-protection authority, reads it the other way: the festival oak died of drought, and the November 1865 planting was already the replacement. So the trunk in front of you is either the 1865 tree, which would make it about 160 years old, or a later stand-in, and nobody has settled which.

Whichever it is, the open ground has suited it. In 1994 it stood 26 metres tall under a crown 20 metres wide, and its girth grew from 3.80 to 4.26 metres between 1994 and 2018. Since 2013 it has had a neighbour it never asked for: the Waldschlösschenbrücke now crosses the river about 25 metres away, and the Elbe cycle path runs past its feet.

trees.name: The Luther Oak of the Dresdner Heide

location.address: Prinzeß-Margarethen-Park, Dresdner Heide, south of Radeberger Landstrasse between forest rides 17 and 18 (Doppel-E to the north, Alte Acht to the south), Forstabteilung 68, Revier Bühlau

trees.access: Free. Stands in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide (Sachsenforst) beside a forest ride, with a memorial stone, two benches and a table; open at all times.
trees.transport: Not verified. About 850 m east of the Fischhaus in the Albertpark and south of Radeberger Landstrasse; likely over 30 minutes from the centre by bus and foot, check timetables before quoting a stop.

Also File:Luthereiche - panoramio.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0, geotag 51.074667,13.806833, 24 March 2011, 12 m from the pin; check the exact photographer credit on the file page). Not viewed by me; the viewing pass must look at the pixels.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the memorial stone with a Luther inscription at its foot, with two benches and a table beside it. It stands on a forest ride in the Prinzeß-Margarethen-Park part of the Heide.
trees.verify_notes: Pin: OSM node 260483097 (natural=tree, name Luthereiche, genus Quercus, tourism=attraction, wikidata Q106253692) at 51.0747442,13.8067087; Wikidata P625 51.0745,13.80665 (about 30 m from the node, rounded to 4 decimals, so the OSM node is used). A geotagged 2011 Commons photo captioned as this tree lies 12 m from the node, and the memorial stone stands beside the tree. Facts (dewiki, citing local sources): planted Sunday 28 Oct 1917 for the 400th anniversary of the Reformation (Luther's 95 Theses); Saxon Kulturdenkmal (ID 09217019) together with the memorial stone. Soil is dry sand over Lusatian granite, so the oak did poorly: called a 'mickriges Exemplar' (puny specimen) in 2017 coverage, so it is NOT a big tree; its worth is the memorial and the setting. Benches renewed and a table added in the 2017 Luther year; one bench carries a Luther quote. Species known only as oak; species not established. Age is the documented 1917 planting of this tree (about 109 years in 2026). No girth or height found. Alive: photographed Feb 2017 and described as living in 2017 coverage; lifecheck not run. One source cluster (dewiki plus OSM plus Commons): flagged. Marginal on worth the walk: young and slight trunk, a lead-grade tree if the photo viewing pass finds it dull.
trees.story:
This oak was planted to honour four hundred years of the Reformation, and it has spent a century failing to look the part. On Sunday 28 October 1917, with Germany deep in the First World War, it went into the ground in the Dresdner Heide to mark the anniversary of Luther's 95 Theses. A memorial stone carrying a Luther inscription was set beside it, and the two together are now a protected Saxon cultural monument, number 09217019.

The ground was against it from the start. This corner of the forest is dry sand over Lusatian granite, and the oak never thrived: local coverage in 2017 called it a puny specimen, which is fair. Nobody comes here for the size of the trunk. What makes it worth the detour is the setting, beside a forest ride in the Prinzeß-Margarethen-Park section of the forest, and the small act of remembrance that keeps being renewed around it. For the Luther year of 2017 the benches were replaced and a table added, and one of the benches now carries a quotation from Luther himself.

It makes a good stop on a walk through the Heide rather than a destination of its own. Two things nobody has recorded: which species of oak it is, and how big it has managed to grow. If you know either, tell us.

trees.name: The Bismarck Oak of the Waldpark Blasewitz

location.address: Waldpark Blasewitz, Lothringer Weg, west of the tennis courts

trees.access: Free. In the Waldpark Blasewitz, a public park; open at all times.
trees.transport: Not verified. Blasewitz, in the Waldpark by the Waldparkrestaurant; check tram stops before quoting a stop.

photo_candidate.note: Description 'Bismarckeiche im Waldpark Blasewitz, Dresden'; sibling File:Bismarckeiche Blasewitz 01.jpg same photographer and date. No geotag on the files. trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the sandstone block beside it, bearing a bronze plaque to the park's designer H. S. Neumann. It stands in a group of trees on the Lothringer Weg, west of the tennis courts.
trees.verify_notes: Register coordinate: de.wikipedia Liste der Gedenkbäume in Dresden gives 51/3/19 N, 13/47/40.5 E (51.05528, 13.79458), identical to Wikidata. OSM node 8551492274 (named Bismarckeiche, Quercus robur, planted=1895) lies at 51.055298,13.7944222, about 11 m west of that point. Two sources agree within about 11 m, but the list says the tree is 'Teil einer Baumgruppe' and the Commons photos have no geotag, so the pin is APPROXIMATE, not confirmed; the photograph is what meets the photo-or-pin requirement. I used the OSM point as the pin. Facts: planted 1895 for Bismarck's 80th birthday; the stone beside it was originally dedicated to Bismarck, its bronze portrait medallion lost shortly after WWII; the existing sandstone block was rededicated in 1998 with a bronze plaque 'Zur Erinnerung an den Gestalter der Waldparkanlage Hofgärtner H. S. Neumann 1829-1880'; no information sign. Age is the documented 1895 planting per the list (about 131 years); no girth or height found. Alive: Commons photos 2017 and the OSM node; lifecheck not run. One source cluster: flagged. Modest as a tree; the draw is the Waldpark and the stone.
trees.story:
The stone beside this oak has changed its mind about who it honours. The tree was planted in 1895 for Otto von Bismarck's 80th birthday, and the sandstone block next to it was dedicated to him too, with his portrait in a bronze medallion. The medallion went missing shortly after the Second World War. In 1998 the block was given a new bronze plaque, this time remembering Hofgärtner H. S. Neumann, 1829 to 1880, the court gardener who designed the Waldpark itself.

So the oak has outlasted the man it was planted for and the monument that explained it. At about 130 years old it is no giant, and nobody has published its girth or height. What it offers is the park its stone now commemorates, and a small lesson in how a memorial gets rewritten when the century moves on.

Be warned before you go: there is no information sign, and the Bismarck Oak stands as part of a group of trees. Our pin is approximate, close to the spot but not on the trunk, so you will have to pick the right oak yourself. The stone is the giveaway. Find the sandstone block with the Neumann plaque on the Lothringer Weg, west of the tennis courts, and the oak is the one beside it.
